claim: Marsupials and placental mammals exhibit significant differences in reproductive and life history strategies.
source: Marsupials and placental mammals exhibit significant differences in reproductive and life history strategies.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about mammalian reproductive strategies.

claim: Marsupials are born highly underdeveloped after an extremely short period of gestation.
source: Marsupials are born highly underdeveloped after an extremely short period of gestation, leading to prioritized development of structures critical for post-birth survival in the pouch.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about marsupial development.

claim: Marsupials must undergo accelerated development of the orofacial region compared to placentals.
source: Critically, they must undergo accelerated development of the orofacial region compared to placentals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research throughout the manuscript.

claim: The fat-tailed dunnart Sminthopsis crassicaudata has one of the shortest gestations of any mammal.
source: Previously, we described the accelerated development of the orofacial region in the carnivorous Australian marsupial, the fat-tailed dunnart Sminthopsis crassicaudata, that has one of the shortest gestations of any mammal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors and established knowledge.

claim: 60,626 putative enhancers and 12,295 putative promoters were identified in the dunnart craniofacial region.
source: This is the first description of genome-wide face regulatory elements in a marsupial, with 60,626 putative enhancers and 12,295 putative promoters described.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: This is the first description of genome-wide face regulatory elements in a marsupial.
source: This is the first description of genome-wide face regulatory elements in a marsupial, with 60,626 putative enhancers and 12,295 putative promoters described.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study, supported by the absence of prior similar studies in the literature.

claim: Genes involved in regulating facial development were largely conserved in mouse and dunnart.
source: While genes involved in regulating facial development were largely conserved in mouse and dunnart, the regulatory landscape varied significantly.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression and regulatory elements between mouse and dunnart presented in the Results section.

claim: The regulatory landscape varied significantly between mouse and dunnart.
source: While genes involved in regulating facial development were largely conserved in mouse and dunnart, the regulatory landscape varied significantly.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative ChIP-seq analysis showing differences in enhancer and promoter activity.

claim: A subset of dunnart-specific enhancers was associated with genes highly expressed only in dunnart relating to cranial neural crest proliferation, embryonic myogenesis, and epidermis development.
source: Additionally, a subset of dunnart-specific enhancers was associated with genes highly expressed only in dunnart relating to cranial neural crest proliferation, embryonic myogenesis, and epidermis development.
evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing dunnart-specific regulatory elements near highly expressed genes.

claim: Comparative RNA-seq analyses of facial tissue revealed dunnart-specific expression of genes involved in the development of the mechanosensory system.
source: Comparative RNA-seq analyses of facial tissue revealed dunnart-specific expression of genes involved in the development of the mechanosensory system.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data comparing gene expression between dunnart and mouse.

claim: Accelerated development of the dunnart sensory system likely relates to the sensory cues received by the nasal–oral region during the postnatal journey to the pouch.
source: Accelerated development of the dunnart sensory system likely relates to the sensory cues received by the nasal–oral region during the postnatal journey to the pouch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene expression patterns and known marsupial biology.

claim: Accelerated face development in the dunnart may be driven by dunnart-specific enhancer activity.
source: Together, these data suggest that accelerated face development in the dunnart may be driven by dunnart-specific enhancer activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing dunnart-specific regulatory elements.

claim: The vertebrate head plays a key role in an organism's ecology by centralizing numerous structures involved in diet, sensory perception, and behavior.
source: The vertebrate head is a highly complex region of the body that plays a key role in an organism's ecology by centralizing numerous structures involved in diet, sensory perception, and behavior (Francis-West and Crespo-Enriquez, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francis-West and Crespo-Enriquez, 2016.

claim: Evolution has modified craniofacial development across lineages, producing a wide array of head morphologies concomitant with the diverse niches that vertebrates occupy.
source: Consequently, evolution has modified craniofacial development across lineages, producing a wide array of head morphologies concomitant with the diverse niches that vertebrates occupy.
evidence: This is supported by established evolutionary biology knowledge.

claim: Placental mammals are characterized by a long gestation with a high maternal investment during pregnancy.
source: Placental mammals are characterized by a long gestation with a high maternal investment during pregnancy, and a considerable degree of both orofacial and neurocranial development occurring in the embryo in utero.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about placental mammal reproduction.

claim: A considerable degree of both orofacial and neurocranial development occurs in the placental embryo in utero.
source: Placental mammals are characterized by a long gestation with a high maternal investment during pregnancy, and a considerable degree of both orofacial and neurocranial development occurring in the embryo in utero.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about placental mammal development.

claim: Placental young experience little functional constraint during early developmental stages.
source: As a result, placental young experience little functional constraint during early developmental stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protected in utero environment of placental mammals.

claim: Marsupials have a short gestation and give birth to highly altricial young that must crawl to the teat.
source: By contrast, marsupials have a short gestation and give birth to highly altricial young that must crawl to the teat, typically located within the maternal pouch, where they complete the remainder of their development ex utero.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about marsupial reproduction.

claim: Marsupials complete the remainder of their development ex utero in the maternal pouch.
source: By contrast, marsupials have a short gestation and give birth to highly altricial young that must crawl to the teat, typically located within the maternal pouch, where they complete the remainder of their development ex utero.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about marsupial development.

claim: The unique reproductive method of marsupials is thought to have imposed strong pressures on the evolution and development of the limbs and head.
source: This unique reproductive method is thought to have imposed strong pressures on the evolution and development of the limbs and head.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on marsupial development.

claim: Marsupials show accelerated development of the nasal cavity, tongue, oral bones, and musculature relative to the development of the posterior end of the body.
source: In particular, marsupials show accelerated development of the nasal cavity, tongue, oral bones, and musculature relative to the development of the posterior end of the body (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 2001a; Cook et al., 2021), and generally when compared to placental embryonic development (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Marsupials show accelerated development of orofacial structures when compared to placental embryonic development.
source: In particular, marsupials show accelerated development of the nasal cavity, tongue, oral bones, and musculature relative to the development of the posterior end of the body (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 2001a; Cook et al., 2021), and generally when compared to placental embryonic development (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Aspects of the peripheral nervous system appear to be accelerated in the marsupial face.
source: Additionally, aspects of the peripheral nervous system appear to be accelerated in the face.
evidence: This is supported by observations described in the manuscript and citations to previous research.

claim: Large medial nasal swellings are observed early in marsupial development that are innervated and proposed to be necessary for the sensory needs of newborn young in their journey to the pouch.
source: We and others have observed large medial nasal swellings early in marsupial development that are innervated and proposed to be necessary for the sensory needs of newborn young in their journey to the pouch (Veitch et al., 2000; Jones and Munger, 1985; Waite et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research including observations by the authors.

claim: Comparative morphometric studies have provided evidence that the difference in craniofacial development has imposed different regimes of constraint on marsupial and placental mammals.
source: Comparative morphometric studies have provided a wealth of evidence that this stark difference in craniofacial development has imposed different regimes of constraint on marsupial and placental mammals (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016) with marsupials in particular showing significantly less interspecies variation in orofacial structures and nasal morphology than placental mammals (Goswami et al., 2016; Sears, 2004; Hüppi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous morphometric studies.

claim: Marsupials show significantly less interspecies variation in orofacial structures and nasal morphology than placental mammals.
source: Comparative morphometric studies have provided a wealth of evidence that this stark difference in craniofacial development has imposed different regimes of constraint on marsupial and placental mammals (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016) with marsupials in particular showing significantly less interspecies variation in orofacial structures and nasal morphology than placental mammals (Goswami et al., 2016; Sears, 2004; Hüppi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that underlie differences in early craniofacial development between marsupial and placental mammals remain poorly understood.
source: In spite of these observations, the molecular mechanisms that underlie these differences in early craniofacial development between marsupial and placental mammals remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cis-acting regulatory regions have been proposed to play a significant role in morphological divergence in the face.
source: Cis-acting regulatory regions have been proposed to play a significant role in morphological divergence in the face, with a number of well-described enhancers that fine-tune face shape in mammals (Attanasio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Attanasio et al., 2013.

claim: There is evidence of a role for regulatory regions in craniofacial heterochrony in marsupials.
source: There is also some evidence of a role for regulatory regions in craniofacial heterochrony in marsupials.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description of a marsupial-specific Sox9 enhancer region.

claim: A marsupial-specific region within a Sox9 enhancer drives early and broad expression in pre-migratory neural crest cell domains contributing to early migration of cranial neural crest cells relative to the mouse.
source: One recent study found a marsupial-specific region within a Sox9 enhancer that drives early and broad expression in pre-migratory neural crest cell domains contributing to early migration of cranial neural crest cells relative to the mouse (Wakamatsu and Suzuki, 2019; Wakamatsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wakamatsu and Suzuki, 2019 and Wakamatsu et al., 2014.

claim: No study has thus far attempted to compare the overall regulatory landscape between marsupials and placentals at developmentally comparable stages.
source: However, no study has thus far attempted to compare the overall regulatory landscape between marsupials and placentals at developmentally comparable stages.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the literature.

claim: The fat-tailed dunnart has emerged as a tractable marsupial model species.
source: In recent years, the fat-tailed dunnart (Sminthopsis crassicaudata, hereafter referred to as the dunnart) has emerged as a tractable marsupial model species (Cook et al., 2021; Suárez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2021 and Suárez et al., 2017.

claim: Dunnarts are born after 13.5 days of gestation.
source: Dunnarts are born after 13.5 days of gestation and craniofacial heterochrony in line with what has been reported in other marsupials is readily observable (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016), making this species an excellent system for comparative studies with placental models.
evidence: This is a factual statement about dunnart gestation supported by established knowledge.

claim: Craniofacial heterochrony in line with what has been reported in other marsupials is readily observable in dunnarts.
source: Dunnarts are born after 13.5 days of gestation and craniofacial heterochrony in line with what has been reported in other marsupials is readily observable (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016), making this species an excellent system for comparative studies with placental models.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dunnarts rely entirely on the advanced chondrocranium with bony elements of the skeleton not present until approximately 24 hr after birth.
source: The dunnart provides an ideal model in which to study the regulatory landscape during craniofacial development in marsupials, as they rely entirely on the advanced chondrocranium with bony elements of the skeleton not present until approximately 24 hr after birth (Cook et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claim: 80,989 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K4me3 were identified in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
source: Peak calling with MACS2 (q < 0.05) identified 80,989 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K4me3 and 121,281 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K27ac in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis described in the Methods and Results.

claim: 121,281 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K27ac were identified in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
source: Peak calling with MACS2 (q < 0.05) identified 80,989 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K4me3 and 121,281 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K27ac in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis described in the Methods and Results.

claim: H3K4me3 often (62% of all H3K4me3 peaks) co-occupied the genome with H3K27ac.
source: Similar to previous studies (Villar et al., 2015; Heintzman et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2013; Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002), we found that H3K4me3 often (62% of all H3K4me3 peaks) co-occupied the genome with H3K27ac (Figure 1A) while 50% of H3K27ac-enriched regions were only associated with this mark (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: 50% of H3K27ac-enriched regions were only associated with this mark.
source: Similar to previous studies (Villar et al., 2015; Heintzman et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2013; Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002), we found that H3K4me3 often (62% of all H3K4me3 peaks) co-occupied the genome with H3K27ac (Figure 1A) while 50% of H3K27ac-enriched regions were only associated with this mark (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Active enhancers are generally enriched for H3K27ac.
source: Active enhancers are generally enriched for H3K27ac (Villar et al., 2015; Creyghton et al., 2010) while sites of transcription initiation (active promoters) can be identified as being marked by both H3K27ac and H3K4me3 (Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Villar et al., 2015 and Creyghton et al., 2010.

claim: Sites of transcription initiation (active promoters) can be identified as being marked by both H3K27ac and H3K4me3.
source: Active enhancers are generally enriched for H3K27ac (Villar et al., 2015; Creyghton et al., 2010) while sites of transcription initiation (active promoters) can be identified as being marked by both H3K27ac and H3K4me3 (Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cain et al., 2011 and Santos-Rosa et al., 2002.

claim: 66,802 promoters and 60,626 enhancers were initially defined in the dunnart.
source: We initially defined promoters as those marked by only H3K4me3 or with >50% of reciprocal peak length for H3K27ac and H3K4me3 peaks, and enhancers as those marked only by H3K27ac, identifying 66,802 promoters and 60,626 enhancers.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis described in the Results.

claim: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS.
source: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS, while promoters were located on average 106 kb from the nearest TSS, despite there being a greater number of peaks located <1 kb from the TSS (1008 enhancers vs. 9023 promoters; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Promoters were located on average 106 kb from the nearest TSS.
source: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS, while promoters were located on average 106 kb from the nearest TSS, despite there being a greater number of peaks located <1 kb from the TSS (1008 enhancers vs. 9023 promoters; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: A large fraction (0.41) of promoters were located >3 kb from an annotated TSS.
source: This was an unexpected finding as a large fraction (0.41) of promoters were located >3 kb from an annotated TSS (see Appendix).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results and Appendix.

claim: H3K4me3 activity at enhancers is well established.
source: H3K4me3 activity at enhancers is well established (Koch and Andrau, 2011; Pekowska et al., 2011); however, compared to H3K4me3 activity at promoters, H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are low (Calo and Wysocka, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koch and Andrau, 2011 and Pekowska et al., 2011.

claim: Compared to H3K4me3 activity at promoters, H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are low.
source: H3K4me3 activity at enhancers is well established (Koch and Andrau, 2011; Pekowska et al., 2011); however, compared to H3K4me3 activity at promoters, H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are low (Calo and Wysocka, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Calo and Wysocka, 2013.

claim: H3K4me3 levels at enhancers were nearly seven times lower than those observed at promoter regions.
source: This is in line with our observations that H3K4me3 levels at enhancers were nearly seven times lower than those observed at promoter regions (see Appendix for details).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results and Appendix.

claim: 12,295 high-confidence promoters were identified after grouping and filtering.
source: Distance from TSS is frequently used to filter putative promoters from other elements, therefore, we grouped peaks characterized as promoters based on their distance to the nearest TSS (see Methods), resulting in 12,295 high-confidence promoters for all of the following analyses (see Appendix).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results and Methods.

claim: 35,677 putative enhancers and 8589 promoters were near genes with a one-to-one ortholog in mouse.
source: To make use of resources available in model organisms such as GO databases, we converted all dunnart gene IDs to mouse orthologous genes for downstream applications. This reduced the dataset to 35,677 putative enhancers and 8589 promoters near (within 1 Mbp) genes with a one-to-one ortholog in mouse (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results.

claim: Gene annotations for both promoters and enhancers were enriched for 23% of the same GO terms.
source: We found that gene annotations for both promoters and enhancers were enriched for 23% of the same GO terms, including cellular processes (protein localization to plasma membrane, protein localization to cell periphery, regulation of cell morphogenesis, positive regulation of cell migration) and development (axon development, camera-type eye development, muscle tissue development, striated muscle development).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis described in the Results.

claim: 44% of GO terms were uniquely enriched among genes assigned to promoters and were related to mRNA processing, transcription, mRNA stability, cell cycle, and mRNA degradation.
source: By contrast, 44% of GO terms were uniquely enriched among genes assigned to promoters and were related to mRNA processing, transcription, mRNA stability, cell cycle, and mRNA degradation (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1b) and uniquely enriched GO terms for genes assigned to candidate enhancers corresponded to processes indicative of early embryonic development (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Uniquely enriched GO terms for genes assigned to candidate enhancers corresponded to processes indicative of early embryonic development.
source: By contrast, 44% of GO terms were uniquely enriched among genes assigned to promoters and were related to mRNA processing, transcription, mRNA stability, cell cycle, and mRNA degradation (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1b) and uniquely enriched GO terms for genes assigned to candidate enhancers corresponded to processes indicative of early embryonic development (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Terms related to facial skeleton development were enriched among genes assigned to putative dunnart enhancers.
source: Terms related to facial skeleton development were enriched among genes assigned to putative dunnart enhancers, including bone cell development, muscle cell development, secondary palate development, roof of mouth development, and mesenchyme development, consistent with dunnart craniofacial morphology (Cook et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claim: Enhancers active near important palate genes in the dunnart at birth may highlight potential regulatory mechanisms driving early palatal closure.
source: Enhancers active near important palate genes (Won et al., 2023; Zarate et al., 2024) such as SHH, SATB2, MEF2C, SNAI2, and IRF6 in the dunnart at birth may highlight potential regulatory mechanisms driving early palatal closure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of enhancers near palate genes and citations to Won et al., 2023 and Zarate et al., 2024.

claim: Terms related to the development of the circulatory system were enriched among genes linked to predicted enhancer regions.
source: In addition, terms related to the development of the circulatory system, including regulation of vasculature development, circulatory system process, and blood circulation were enriched among genes linked to predicted enhancer regions (e.g., ACE, PDGFB, GATA4, GATA6, VEGFA).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis described in the Results.

claim: The oral region of newborn dunnarts is highly vascularized, with blood vessels visible through their translucent skin at birth.
source: This is consistent with observations that show the oral region of newborn dunnarts is highly vascularized, with blood vessels visible through their translucent skin at birth (Cook et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claim: Enhancers were significantly enriched for 170 TFs relative to a background set of random GC- and length-matched sequences.
source: Enhancers were significantly enriched for 170 TFs relative to a background set of random GC- and length-matched sequences (FDR-corrected, p < 0.01), including those with known roles in differentiation of cranial neural crest cells (TWIST, HOXA2), skeletal morphogenesis (DLX5, CREB5, HOXA2), bone development (ATF3, RUNX), cranial nerve development (ATOH1), and/or facial mesenchyme development (LHX2, FOXP1, MAFB; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the motif enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: TFBS in promoter sequences were dominated by transcriptional initiation regulatory sequences, with significant enrichment for 13 TFs.
source: Consistent with the GO enrichment, TFBS in promoter sequences were dominated by transcriptional initiation regulatory sequences, with significant enrichment for 13 TFs (FDR-corrected, p < 0.01) including RFX3, RFX2, NRF, NRF1, GRY, ZBTB33, RONIN, JUND, and GFX (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the motif enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: There were 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed at a level >1 TPM across three biological replicates in dunnart face tissue.
source: There were 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed at a level >1 TPM across three biological replicates, with the majority of genes expressed (67%; 8158/12,153) associated with an active enhancer and/or promoter peak.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis described in the Results.

claim: The majority of genes expressed (67%; 8158/12,153) were associated with an active enhancer and/or promoter peak.
source: There were 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed at a level >1 TPM across three biological replicates, with the majority of genes expressed (67%; 8158/12,153) associated with an active enhancer and/or promoter peak.
evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Most enhancers (78% of all enhancers) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart.
source: Most enhancers (78% of all enhancers, Supplementary file 1d) or promoters (87% of all promoters, Supplementary file 1e) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Most promoters (87% of all promoters) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart.
source: Most enhancers (78% of all enhancers, Supplementary file 1d) or promoters (87% of all promoters, Supplementary file 1e) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of reproducibly expressed genes near a regulatory peak (61%) were associated with both an enhancer and promoter region.
source: Additionally, the majority of reproducibly expressed genes near a regulatory peak (61%) were associated with both an enhancer and promoter region (Figure 3B), highlighting the correspondence in active regulatory elements and expressed genes at this time point in the dunnart face.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Genes with a medium-to-high expression level (>10 TPM) and associated with at least one putative enhancer and promoter were enriched for biological processes including 'in utero embryonic development', 'skeletal system development', 'muscle tissue development', 'skin development', 'vasculature development', and 'sensory organ development'.
source: Genes with a medium-to-high expression level at this stage (>10 TPM) and associated with at least one putative enhancer and promoter were enriched for biological processes including 'in utero embryonic development', 'skeletal system development', 'muscle tissue development', 'skin development', 'vasculature development', and 'sensory organ development' (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Enrichment for the term 'in utero embryonic development' is indicative of the altricial nature of the dunnart neonate.
source: Enrichment for the term 'in utero embryonic development' is indicative of the altricial nature of the dunnart neonate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GO enrichment results and knowledge of dunnart development.

claim: In the dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (day of birth young corresponding approximately to embryonic day (E) 12.5 in mouse).
source: In a previous study, we showed that in the dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (day of birth young corresponding approximately to embryonic day (E) 12.5 in mouse) and that the dunnart neonate instead likely relies on the well-developed cranial muscles and an extremely large chondrocranium for structural head and feeding support during early pouch life (Cook et al., 2021; Clark and Smith, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2021 and Clark and Smith, 1993.

claim: The dunnart neonate likely relies on the well-developed cranial muscles and an extremely large chondrocranium for structural head and feeding support during early pouch life.
source: In a previous study, we showed that in the dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (day of birth young corresponding approximately to embryonic day (E) 12.5 in mouse) and that the dunnart neonate instead likely relies on the well-developed cranial muscles and an extremely large chondrocranium for structural head and feeding support during early pouch life (Cook et al., 2021; Clark and Smith, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2021 and Clark and Smith, 1993.

claim: High expression (>20 TPM) of key head myogenesis genes was observed in the dunnart.
source: Consistent with this, we observed high expression (>20 TPM) of the key head myogenesis genes (Bentzinger et al., 2012; Buckingham, 2017; Lin et al., 2006), MYOD1, MYF6, MEF2C, PAX3, MYL1, and MYOG, essential genes regulating chondrogenesis (Lefebvre et al., 2019; Yip et al., 2019), SOX9, COL2A1, and FGFR1 and genes that act upstream of osteoblast differentiation (Qi et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2007), MSX1, MSX2, CEBPA/G, ALPL, DLX3, DLX5, FGFR1, and FGFR2 (Supplementary file 1d, e).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data and citations to previous research.

claim: Craniofacial development in the newborn dunnart is approximately equivalent to E12.5 in mouse.
source: From our morphological study of dunnart craniofacial bone development, we estimated that craniofacial development in the newborn dunnart is approximately equivalent to E12.5 in mouse (Cook et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claim: ~17K enhancers and ~10K promoters per stage were found in the mouse after applying consistent peak calling and filtering parameters.
source: After applying consistent peak calling and filtering parameters to the dunnart ChIP-seq data, we found ~17K enhancers and ~10K promoters per stage in the mouse (Figure 4A, see Appendix for details).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of mouse ENCODE data described in the Results.

claim: The features of mouse predicted enhancer and promoters were consistent with the observations in the dunnart.
source: The features of mouse predicted enhancer and promoters (percentage CpG, GC content, distance from TSS, peak length, and peak intensity) were consistent with the observations in the dunnart (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis and data presented in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The alignability (conserved sequence) for dunnart enhancers to the mouse genome was ~13% for 100 bp regions.
source: The alignability (conserved sequence) for dunnart enhancers to the mouse genome was ~13% for 100 bp regions (Supplementary file 1v).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-genome alignment analysis described in the Results.

claim: Between 0.74% and 6.77% of enhancer regions out of all alignable enhancers were present in both mouse and dunnart.
source: Between 0.74% and 6.77% of enhancer regions out of all alignable enhancers were present in both mouse and dunnart (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements.

claim: Between 45% and 57% of alignable promoter regions were present in mouse and dunnart.
source: In contrast, between 45% and 57% of alignable promoter regions were present in mouse and dunnart (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements.

claim: Promoter regions are more stable over large evolutionary distances than enhancers.
source: Although this is a small fraction of the total peaks (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers; Supplementary file 1g), it suggests that, consistent with the literature (Villar et al., 2015), promoter regions are more stable over large evolutionary distances and that shifts in developmental timing of craniofacial marsupials may be more likely to be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions in marsupials.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data and citation to Villar et al., 2015.

claim: Shifts in developmental timing of craniofacial marsupials may be more likely to be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions in marsupials.
source: Although this is a small fraction of the total peaks (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers; Supplementary file 1g), it suggests that, consistent with the literature (Villar et al., 2015), promoter regions are more stable over large evolutionary distances and that shifts in developmental timing of craniofacial marsupials may be more likely to be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions in marsupials.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data.

claim: Regions with conserved activity between mouse and dunnart were predominantly near genes consistently expressed in both and were enriched for core craniofacial developmental and signaling processes.
source: Despite this, regions with conserved activity between the two species were predominantly near genes consistently expressed in both and were enriched for core craniofacial developmental and signaling processes.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claim: Predicted dunnart enhancers with sequence conservation in mouse and matching peak activity at any of the five mouse embryonic stages (461 regions) were located near genes reproducibly expressed (>1 TPM, 89%) in both species.
source: Predicted dunnart enhancers with sequence conservation in mouse and matching peak activity at any of the five mouse embryonic stages (461 regions) were located near genes reproducibly expressed (>1 TPM, 89%) in both species (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claim: Genes near conserved enhancers were enriched for core developmental and signaling processes: BMP signaling, cartilage development, ossification, skeletal development, and chondrocyte differentiation.
source: Genes in this group were enriched for core developmental and signaling processes: BMP signaling, cartilage development, ossification, skeletal development, and chondrocyte differentiation (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis of genes near conserved enhancers.

claim: For the 4311 dunnart-specific enhancers, 2310 (54%) were linked to genes expressed >1 TPM in all stages and species.
source: Taking the predicted dunnart enhancers alignable to the mouse but without a matching peak, we looked at nearby genes and compared expression between mouse and dunnart. For the 4311 dunnart-specific enhancers, we found that 2310 (54%) were linked to genes expressed >1 TPM in all stages and species, suggesting that these genes in mouse could be regulated by a different set of regulatory regions or could be accounted for by the reduced enrichment in the mouse ENCODE ChIP-seq face datasets for H3K27ac (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claim: A smaller subset (179 regions, 114 unique genes) of dunnart-specific enhancers were near genes highly expressed (>10 TPM) only in the dunnart with low to no activity in the mouse at any of the embryonic stages.
source: We found a smaller subset (179 regions, 114 unique genes) where the nearest genes were highly expressed (>10 TPM) only in the dunnart with low to no activity in the mouse at any of the embryonic stages (E10.5–E15.5; Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claim: Dunnart-specific enhancers near highly expressed genes included genes involved in cranial neural crest proliferation and migration (INKA2, TFAP2E, OVOL2, GPR161).
source: This included genes involved in cranial neural crest proliferation and migration (INKA2, TFAP2E, OVOL2, GPR161), keratinocyte proliferation (PLAU, HOXA1), embryonic myogenesis (PDF4), development of the ectodermal placodes and sensory systems (CNGA2, ELF5, EDN1, HOXA1, ATOH1, NPHP4, CFD, WNT2B) and vomeronasal sensory neuron development (TFAP2E; Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claim: The largest intersection size in genes with putative promoters was between the six mouse embryonic stages (1910 genes; 21.2%).
source: The largest intersection size in genes with putative promoters was between the six mouse embryonic stages (1910 genes; 21.2%) and between the dunnart all six embryonic mouse stages (1908 genes, 21.2%; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the gene-level comparison presented in Figure 5A.

claim: 4483 predicted target genes (56%) near enhancers were unique to the dunnart at D0.
source: Overlap between enhancers was more restricted, with 4483 predicted target genes (56%) being unique to the dunnart at D0 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the gene-level comparison presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The top enriched terms for biological processes were largely shared across dunnart and mouse, with the exception of one GO term, 'sensory system development'.
source: The top enriched terms for biological processes were largely shared across dunnart and mouse, with the exception of one GO term, 'sensory system development' (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genes highly expressed in dunnart but lowly or not expressed in mouse (537 total) were related to three main developmental processes: 'epidermis/skin development and keratinization', 'sensory system development', and 'muscle development and contraction'.
source: Genes highly expressed in dunnart but lowly or not expressed in mouse (537 total; see Supplementary file 1k) were related to three main developmental processes, 'epidermis/skin development and keratinization', 'sensory system development', and 'muscle development and contraction' (Figure 5C, D; Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative gene expression analysis and GO enrichment presented in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Genes critical for development of keratinocytes and the establishment of a skin barrier were highly expressed in dunnart facial tissue with lower expression or no transcripts expressed across the mouse embryonic stages.
source: Genes critical for development of keratinocytes and the establishment of a skin barrier were highly expressed in dunnart facial tissue with lower expression or no transcripts expressed across the mouse embryonic stages including IGFBP2, SFN, AQP3, HOPX, KRT17, KRT7, KRT8, and KRT78 (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Keratin genes are critical for the development of the mammalian mechanosensory system.
source: Keratin genes are also critical for the development of the mammalian mechanosensory system (Xiao et al., 2014; Doucet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2014 and Doucet et al., 2013.

claim: Krt17-expressing epidermal keratinocytes are necessary to establish innervation patterns during development.
source: Krt17-expressing epidermal keratinocytes are necessary to establish innervation patterns during development, and Krt8 and Atoh1 expression is required for the specification of the Merkel cells (touch sensory cells) (Doucet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Doucet et al., 2013.

claim: Krt8 and Atoh1 expression is required for the specification of the Merkel cells (touch sensory cells).
source: Krt17-expressing epidermal keratinocytes are necessary to establish innervation patterns during development, and Krt8 and Atoh1 expression is required for the specification of the Merkel cells (touch sensory cells) (Doucet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Doucet et al., 2013.

claim: KRT17, ATOH1, and KRT8 are all very highly expressed in dunnart compared to the low expression in mouse facial tissue.
source: KRT17, ATOH1, and KRT8 are all very highly expressed in dunnart compared to the low expression in mouse facial tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative gene expression analysis.

claim: High expression of genes involved in development of the olfactory system was observed in the dunnart including CCK, OTX1, and ISLR.
source: Additionally, we observed high expression of genes involved in development of the olfactory system including CCK, OTX1, and ISLR (expressed in olfactory epithelium) (Liu and Liu, 2018; Simeone, 1998; Santoro and Jakob, 2018; Haering et al., 2015), and Ybx3 (Haering et al., 2015) (expressed in the nasal epithelium; Figure 5D, Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data and citations to previous research.

claim: Muscle contraction genes such as TNNI2 and TNNT3 were upregulated in dunnart craniofacial tissue.
source: Muscle contraction genes such as TNNI2 (Robinson et al., 2007) and TNNT3 (Wei and Jin, 2016; Sung et al., 2003) and genes involved in skeletal muscle development (Jung and Ko, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Feng and Jin, 2016; Aboalola and Han, 2017) (CAR3, ATP2A2, IGFBP6, and TRIM72) were upregulated in dunnart craniofacial tissue (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data and citations to previous research.

claim: The majority of conserved toolkit genes involved in embryonic development had consistent expression across mouse and dunnart.
source: The majority of conserved toolkit genes involved in embryonic development had consistent expression across mouse and dunnart (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dunnart expressed genes were associated with a set of genes upregulated specifically at E15.5 in mouse (cluster 2: OR = 1.30, CI = 1.15–1.46).
source: Although dunnart facial development more closely resembles approximately E12.5 (Cook et al., 2021) in the mouse, when compared to the temporal gene expression dynamics during mouse craniofacial, dunnart expressed genes were associated with two distinct clusters: a set of genes upregulated specifically at E15.5 in mouse (cluster 2: OR = 1.30, CI = 1.15–1.46; Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and a set of genes upregulated at E14.5 (cluster 3: OR = 1.99; CI = 1.78–2.24; Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the temporal clustering analysis presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dunnart expressed genes were associated with a set of genes upregulated at E14.5 in mouse (cluster 3: OR = 1.99; CI = 1.78–2.24).
source: Although dunnart facial development more closely resembles approximately E12.5 (Cook et al., 2021) in the mouse, when compared to the temporal gene expression dynamics during mouse craniofacial, dunnart expressed genes were associated with two distinct clusters: a set of genes upregulated specifically at E15.5 in mouse (cluster 2: OR = 1.30, CI = 1.15–1.46; Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and a set of genes upregulated at E14.5 (cluster 3: OR = 1.99; CI = 1.78–2.24; Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the temporal clustering analysis presented in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cluster 2 genes were enriched for functions related to sensory perception, skin development, and keratinization.
source: Cluster 2 genes were enriched for functions related to sensory perception, skin development, and keratinization (Figure 6C), while cluster 3 genes were enriched for muscle development (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Cluster 3 genes were enriched for muscle development.
source: Cluster 2 genes were enriched for functions related to sensory perception, skin development, and keratinization (Figure 6C), while cluster 3 genes were enriched for muscle development (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Shifts in the developmental timing of the skin, muscle, and sensory perception may play a role in marsupial early life history.
source: These results align with our observations in dunnart enhancer and gene expression data, suggesting that shifts in the developmental timing of the skin, muscle, and sensory perception may play a role in marsupial early life history.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal clustering analysis and comparative gene expression data.

claim: Marsupials display advanced development of the orofacial region relative to development of the central nervous system when compared to placental mammals.
source: Marsupials display advanced development of the orofacial region relative to development of the central nervous system when compared to placental mammals (Smith, 2006; Smith, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith, 2006 and Smith, 1997.

claim: The facial skeleton and muscular tissues begin development early relative to the neurocranium differentiation in marsupials.
source: Specifically, the facial skeleton and muscular tissues begin development early relative to the neurocranium differentiation (Smith, 2006; Smith, 1997; Clark and Smith, 1993; Smith, 1999; Smith, 2001b; Smith, 2003; Sánchez-Villagra and Forasiepi, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Development of the central nervous system is protracted in marsupials compared to placentals.
source: Although development of the central nervous system is protracted in marsupials compared to placentals, marsupials have well-developed peripheral motor nerves and sensory nerves (e.g., the trigeminal) at birth (Karlen and Krubitzer, 2007; Smith and Keyte, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karlen and Krubitzer, 2007 and Smith and Keyte, 2020.

claim: Marsupials have well-developed peripheral motor nerves and sensory nerves (e.g., the trigeminal) at birth.
source: Although development of the central nervous system is protracted in marsupials compared to placentals, marsupials have well-developed peripheral motor nerves and sensory nerves (e.g., the trigeminal) at birth (Karlen and Krubitzer, 2007; Smith and Keyte, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karlen and Krubitzer, 2007 and Smith and Keyte, 2020.

claim: The genetic drivers of variation in craniofacial development between mammalian species are largely unexplored.
source: Despite increasing descriptions of craniofacial enhancers in model species (Attanasio et al., 2013; Brinkley et al., 2016; Samuels et al., 2020; Prescott et al., 2015; Rajderkar et al., 2024), the genetic drivers of variation in craniofacial development between mammalian species are largely unexplored.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Regulatory elements in the dunnart were largely not sequence conserved in the mouse (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers).
source: Given the large evolutionary distance (~170 million years) between the mouse and dunnart (Bininda-Emonds et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2011) and high turnover of non-coding DNA sequences (Genereux et al., 2020; Andrews et al., 2023), regulatory elements in the dunnart were largely not sequence conserved in the mouse (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis and citations to previous research on evolutionary distance and sequence turnover.

claim: Despite differences in experimental methods, when taking a gene-level approach, there was significant overlap in genes near regulatory elements in both species.
source: Moreover, despite differences in experimental methods, when taking a gene-level approach, there was significant overlap in genes near regulatory elements in both species, with high concordance in enriched biological process terms.
evidence: This is supported by the gene-level comparative analysis.

claim: Conserved genes and signaling pathways are crucial for mammalian facial development.
source: This supports the notion that conserved genes and signaling pathways are crucial for mammalian facial development (Roosenboom et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roosenboom et al., 2016.

claim: In marsupials, pharyngeal muscles are well differentiated before birth preceding development of both the central nervous system and the skeletal system.
source: In marsupials, pharyngeal muscles are well differentiated before birth preceding development of both the central nervous system and the skeletal system (Smith, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith, 1994.

claim: In the first 2 days immediately after birth, marsupial pouch young undergo considerable differentiation of the facial muscles.
source: Additionally, in the first 2 days immediately after birth, marsupial pouch young undergo considerable differentiation of the facial muscles (Smith, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith, 1994.

claim: In rodents, the events of skeletal and muscular development generally occur simultaneously.
source: This pattern varies significantly from rodents where the events of skeletal and muscular development generally occur simultaneously (Smith, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith, 1994.

claim: Newborn dunnarts exhibit high expression of KRT17 in the face and other genes essential for periderm establishment and maintenance.
source: Newborn dunnarts exhibit high expression of KRT17 in the face and other genes essential for periderm establishment and maintenance (Hammond et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016; Noiret et al., 2016; Kousa et al., 2017; Carroll, 2024; Vaziri Sani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data and citations to previous research.

claim: Unlike placental mammals, marsupials retain the periderm post-birth.
source: Unlike placental mammals, marsupials retain the periderm post-birth (Smith and Keyte, 2020; Lillegraven, 1975; Pralomkarn et al., 1990), which may relate to neonatal transcutaneous gas exchange observed in marsupials in the first few days after birth (Simpson et al., 2011; Ferner, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Retention of the periderm in marsupials may relate to neonatal transcutaneous gas exchange observed in marsupials in the first few days after birth.
source: Unlike placental mammals, marsupials retain the periderm post-birth (Smith and Keyte, 2020; Lillegraven, 1975; Pralomkarn et al., 1990), which may relate to neonatal transcutaneous gas exchange observed in marsupials in the first few days after birth (Simpson et al., 2011; Ferner, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to previous research.

claim: In placental mammals such as mouse and human, the periderm only exists in utero and disappears late in gestation with the eruption of hair and the development of a thick keratinized stratum corneum.
source: In placental mammals such as mouse and human, the periderm only exists in utero and disappears late in gestation with the eruption of hair and the development of a thick keratinized stratum corneum (Hammond et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hammond et al., 2019.

claim: Dunnarts rely heavily on gas exchange through the skin and only begin lung respiration around 5 days postpartum, coinciding with the disappearance of the periderm.
source: The persistence of the periderm aligns with the observation that dunnarts rely heavily on gas exchange through the skin and only begin lung respiration around 5 days postpartum, coinciding with the disappearance of the periderm (Simpson et al., 2011; Krause et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Simpson et al., 2011 and Krause et al., 1978.

claim: Newborn marsupial young require highly developed sensory systems (mechanosensory and olfactory systems) to respond to the cues that guide them to the teat inside the mother's pouch.
source: Newborn marsupial young require highly developed sensory systems (mechanosensory and olfactory systems) to respond to the cues that guide them to the teat inside the mother's pouch, with the nasal-oral region making regular contact with the mother's belly during the crawl to the pouch (Waite et al., 1994; Desmarais et al., 2016; Gemmell and Nelson, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The snout epidermis of newborn marsupials has been shown to be innervated with the presence of mature Merkel cells with connected nerve terminals.
source: The snout epidermis of newborn marsupials has been shown to be innervated with the presence of mature Merkel cells with connected nerve terminals (Veitch et al., 2000; Jones and Munger, 1985; Desmarais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the mouse, Merkel cell development does not begin until later at approximately E16.5.
source: In the mouse, Merkel cell development does not begin until later at approximately E16.5 (Jenkins et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jenkins et al., 2019.

claim: Upregulation of Merkel cell genes in dunnart facial tissue could be a result of prioritization of sensory development required for life outside the womb in a highly underdeveloped state.
source: Upregulation of Merkel cell genes in dunnart facial tissue could be a result of prioritization of sensory development required for life outside the womb in a highly underdeveloped state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data and knowledge of marsupial biology.

claim: Craniofacial developmental constraints in the dunnart may be driven by dunnart-specific gene regulation.
source: In summary, our work suggests that craniofacial developmental constraints in the dunnart may be driven by dunnart-specific gene regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of all the data presented in the study.

claim: The dunnart genome assembly had a total size of 2.84 Gb and an N50 length of 23 megabases (Mb).
source: The resulting genome assembly had a total size of 2.84 Gb and an N50 length of 23 megabases (Mb).
evidence: This is supported by the genome assembly described in the Methods.

claim: BUSCO gene recovery was 89.9% for complete orthologs in the mammalia_odb10 lineage dataset.
source: BUSCO gene recovery was 89.9% for complete orthologs in the mammalia_odb10 lineage dataset which includes 9226 BUSCOs.
evidence: This is supported by the BUSCO analysis described in the Methods.

claim: The assembly is of comparable completeness and contiguity to other recently published marsupial genomes.
source: Together, these metrics indicate that the assembly is of comparable completeness and contiguity to other recently published marsupial genomes (Feigin et al., 2018; Feigin et al., 2022; Renfree et al., 2011; Murchison et al., 2012; Mikkelsen et al., 2007; Peel et al., 2021; Brandies et al., 2020) and therefore represents an excellent resource for downstream functional genomic experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the assembly metrics and citations to other marsupial genomes.

claim: The G+C content of the de novo contigs in the dunnart was ~36.25%.
source: The G+C content of the de novo contigs in the dunnart (~36.25%) was similar to other marsupial species Tasmanian devil: 36.4% (Murchison et al., 2012), thylacine: ~36% (Feigin et al., 2018), wallaby: 34–38.8% (Renfree et al., 2011), opossum: 37.8% (Mikkelsen et al., 2007), woylie: 38.6% (Peel et al., 2021), and the brown antechinus: 36.2% (Brandies et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the genome assembly analysis and citations to other marsupial genomes.
